subject: math
title: Geometry II: Volume, Surface Area, and Scale
objectives: Students will read the GED formula sheet and identify what B, p, h, s, and r stand for in each formula.
Students will find the volume and surface area of rectangular prisms and cylinders.
Students will find the volume and surface area of pyramids and cones, choosing height or slant height correctly.
Students will find the volume and surface area of spheres, including problems that give the diameter.
Students will use scale drawings and scale factors to find actual lengths, areas, and volumes.
teach:
Objectives

  • Read the GED formula sheet and say what each letter means, especially B (area of the base), p (perimeter of the base), h (height), s (slant height), and r (radius).
  • Find the volume and surface area of rectangular prisms and cylinders.
  • Find the volume and surface area of pyramids and cones, choosing height or slant height correctly.
  • Find the volume and surface area of spheres.
  • Use scale drawings and scale factors to find actual lengths, areas, and volumes.

Materials

  • A printed copy of the GED Mathematical Reasoning formula sheet for every student (free on the official GED website), or the formula box on this week's Study Sheet
  • Everyday solids to hold up: a cereal box (rectangular prism), a soup can (cylinder), a party hat or ice cream cone (cone), a ball (sphere), and, if you have one, a pyramid-shaped paperweight or a folded paper pyramid
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet
  • Scientific calculators with a π key (the GED on-screen calculator has one)
  • Scratch paper, rulers, and highlighters

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick area and perimeter problems from Week 5. These are the building blocks for B and p.
Direct instruction20Reading the formula sheet (4 min), prisms and cylinders (6 min), pyramids and cones (5 min), spheres (2 min), scale drawings and scale factors (3 min).
Guided practice15Six problems worked with the class; students say which formula and which measurements they will use before computing.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–8 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, preview of the exit ticket, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Post these as students arrive. Tell them that every formula today is built from these Week 5 skills.

  1. Area of a rectangle 8 ft by 5 ft
  2. Perimeter of the same rectangle
  3. Area of a triangle with base 6 in and height 4 in
  4. Area of a circle with radius 3 cm (use 3.14 for π)
  5. Circumference of the same circle (use 3.14 for π)

Answers: (1) 8 × 5 = 40 ft2   (2) 2(8) + 2(5) = 26 ft   (3) ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 in2   (4) 3.14 × 32 = 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 cm2   (5) 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 cm

Point out that problems 1 and 4 are areas of a base (B) and problems 2 and 5 are perimeters of a base (p). Today we stack those flat shapes up into solids.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. Volume, surface area, and the formula sheet (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Hold up the cereal box. Volume is how much the box holds: the space inside, measured in cubic units (in3, ft3, cm3). Surface area is how much cardboard it takes to make the box: the total area of every outside face, measured in square units (in2, ft2).
  • Students do not need to memorize these formulas. The GED gives a formula sheet during the math test. The skill being tested is reading the sheet correctly and plugging in the right measurements.
  • Walk through the letters on the sheet with this table. Have students highlight each letter on their copy as you go.
LetterMeaningHow to get it
BArea of the base (a flat area)Use the area formula for the base shape: rectangle lw, square s2, circle πr2, triangle ½bh
pPerimeter of the base (a length)Add all the sides of the base; a square base is 4 × side
hHeightThe straight-up distance from the base to the top or tip, at a right angle to the base
sSlant heightThe distance from the tip down the slanted side to the edge of the base (pyramids and cones only)
rRadiusHalf the diameter
πPi, about 3.14Use the π key or 3.14, whichever the question says

Then show the five solid formulas and the patterns that tie them together:

SolidVolumeSurface area
Rectangular/right prismV = BhSA = ph + 2B
CylinderV = πr2hSA = 2πrh + 2πr2
PyramidV = (1/3)BhSA = ½ps + B
ConeV = (1/3)πr2hSA = πrs + πr2
SphereV = (4/3)πr3SA = 4πr2
  • Pattern 1: A cylinder is a prism with a circle for a base, so πr2h is just B × h with B = πr2.
  • Pattern 2: A pyramid holds exactly 1/3 of the prism with the same base and height, and a cone holds 1/3 of the matching cylinder. That is where the 1/3 comes from.
  • Pattern 3: In every surface-area formula, the “B” or “πr2” part is the base or bases. Prisms and cylinders have two bases (+ 2B), and pyramids and cones have one (+ B). The rest of the formula is the sides.
  • Pattern 4: Volume formulas use h. Only the surface-area formulas for pyramids and cones use s.

2. Prisms and cylinders (about 6 minutes)

Worked Example 1 (rectangular prism). A shipping box is 10 inches long, 6 inches wide, and 4 inches tall. Find its volume and its surface area.

Volume, V = Bh. The base is a 10 by 6 rectangle: B = 10 × 6 = 60 in2

V = 60 × 4 = 240 in3

Surface area, SA = ph + 2B. Perimeter of the base: p = 2(10) + 2(6) = 20 + 12 = 32 in

ph = 32 × 4 = 128 in2 (the four side faces)

2B = 2 × 60 = 120 in2 (top and bottom)

SA = 128 + 120 = 248 in2

Check by adding the six faces: 2(10 × 6) + 2(10 × 4) + 2(6 × 4) = 120 + 80 + 48 = 248 in2.

Answers: V = 240 in3; SA = 248 in2

Worked Example 2 (cylinder). A can has a diameter of 6 cm and a height of 10 cm. Use 3.14 for π. Find its volume and surface area.

First, the radius: r = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm

Volume: V = πr2h = 3.14 × 32 × 10 = 3.14 × 9 × 10 = 282.6 cm3

Surface area: SA = 2πrh + 2πr2

2πrh = 2 × 3.14 × 3 × 10 = 188.4 cm2 (the label around the side)

2πr2 = 2 × 3.14 × 9 = 56.52 cm2 (top and bottom lids)

SA = 188.4 + 56.52 = 244.92 cm2

Answers: V = 282.6 cm3; SA = 244.92 cm2. Ask: what goes wrong if someone uses 6 as the radius? (The volume becomes 1,130.4, four times too big.)

3. Pyramids and cones (about 5 minutes)

Talking points: Hold up the cone. Run one finger straight down the middle from the tip to the center of the base (that is h), then down the outside edge (that is s). The slant height is always longer than the height, because it is the long side (hypotenuse) of a right triangle. If a problem gives both, students must pick the right one for the formula.

Worked Example 3 (square pyramid). A square pyramid has base edges of 6 m, a height of 4 m, and a slant height of 5 m. Find its volume and surface area.

Base: B = 6 × 6 = 36 m2. Perimeter of the base: p = 4 × 6 = 24 m.

Volume uses the height: V = (1/3)Bh = (1/3) × 36 × 4 = 12 × 4 = 48 m3

Surface area uses the slant height: SA = ½ps + B = ½ × 24 × 5 + 36 = 60 + 36 = 96 m2

Check: the four triangle faces each have area ½ × 6 × 5 = 15, and 4 × 15 = 60. Add the square base, 36, to get 96.

Answers: V = 48 m3; SA = 96 m2

Worked Example 4 (cone). A cone has radius 3 in, height 4 in, and slant height 5 in. Use 3.14 for π.

Volume (uses h): V = (1/3)πr2h = (1/3) × 3.14 × 9 × 4 = 3.14 × 12 = 37.68 in3

Surface area (uses s): SA = πrs + πr2 = 3.14 × 3 × 5 + 3.14 × 9 = 47.1 + 28.26 = 75.36 in2

Answers: V = 37.68 in3; SA = 75.36 in2

4. Spheres (about 2 minutes)

Talking points: A sphere has only one measurement, the radius. Watch for problems that give the diameter of a ball or tank. Remind students that r3 means r × r × r, not 3r.

Worked Example 5 (sphere). A ball has a diameter of 10 cm. Use 3.14 for π. Find its surface area and its volume to the nearest tenth.

r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm

SA = 4πr2 = 4 × 3.14 × 25 = 314 cm2

V = (4/3)πr3 = (4/3) × 3.14 × 125 = 4 × 3.14 × 125 ÷ 3 = 1,570 ÷ 3 ≈ 523.3 cm3

Calculator tip: multiply everything on top first, then divide by 3 last.

Answers: SA = 314 cm2; V ≈ 523.3 cm3

5. Scale drawings and scale factors (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A scale such as 1 in : 4 ft means every inch on the drawing stands for 4 feet in real life. Set up a proportion or simply multiply each drawing length by 4.
  • Convert lengths first, then compute area or volume from the real lengths. This avoids the most common error.
  • When every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, perimeter is multiplied by k, area by k2, and volume by k3.

Worked Example 6 (scale drawing). On a floor plan, the scale is 1 inch : 4 feet. A bedroom measures 3.5 inches by 2.75 inches on the plan. What are the actual dimensions and the actual floor area?

Length: 3.5 × 4 = 14 ft. Width: 2.75 × 4 = 11 ft.

Area: 14 × 11 = 154 ft2

Check with the area rule: drawing area = 3.5 × 2.75 = 9.625 in2; scale factor 4, so area factor 42 = 16; 9.625 × 16 = 154 ft2. Multiplying 9.625 by only 4 (38.5) is the classic mistake.

Quick extension: a 2-inch cube has volume 23 = 8 in3. Double every edge to 4 inches: 43 = 64 in3, which is 8 times as much, because 23 = 8.

Answers: 14 ft by 11 ft; 154 ft2

Teacher note: If time is short, model Examples 1, 3, and 6 fully, and let students try Examples 2 and 5 with a partner. Insist that students write the formula first, then the formula with numbers substituted, then the answer with units. That three-line habit prevents most errors.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

For each problem, have a student name the formula and the measurements to use before anyone computes. Use 3.14 for π.

  1. A cube has edges of 5 cm. Find its volume and surface area.
  2. A cylindrical planter has a diameter of 8 ft and a height of 5 ft. Find its volume.
  3. A cone has a radius of 3 m and a height of 7 m. Find its volume.
  4. A sphere has a diameter of 6 in. Find its volume.
  5. A pyramid has a rectangular base 9 ft by 4 ft and a height of 10 ft. Find its volume.
  6. A map scale is 1 cm : 25 km. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they?

Answers with steps:

1. B = 5 × 5 = 25; V = Bh = 25 × 5 = 125 cm3. p = 4 × 5 = 20; SA = ph + 2B = 20 × 5 + 2 × 25 = 100 + 50 = 150 cm2 (six faces of 25 each).

2. r = 4; V = 3.14 × 42 × 5 = 3.14 × 16 × 5 = 251.2 ft3.

3. V = (1/3) × 3.14 × 9 × 7 = 3.14 × 21 = 65.94 m3.

4. r = 3; V = (4/3) × 3.14 × 27 = 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 in3.

5. B = 9 × 4 = 36; V = (1/3) × 36 × 10 = 120 ft3.

6. 6.4 × 25 = 160 km.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students open this week's 12 practice items and complete items 1–8 in class. Items 9–12 are multi-step problems (scale factors and a composite solid); students finish them at home. Ask struggling students two questions before giving a hint: “Which solid is it?” and “Which letters does that formula need?”

Checks for Understanding

  • What does B stand for, and what is B for a cylinder? Expected: area of the base; for a cylinder, πr2.
  • What does p stand for in SA = ph + 2B? Expected: the perimeter of the base, a length, not an area.
  • For the volume of a cone, do you use the height or the slant height? Expected: the height. Slant height appears only in the surface-area formulas for pyramids and cones.
  • A tank's diameter is 12 ft. What number goes in for r? Expected: 6.
  • Every edge of a box is tripled. How many times larger is the volume? Expected: 33 = 27 times.
  • Is paint for a wall a volume or a surface-area question? Expected: surface area (it covers the outside).

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Using the diameter as the radius. A student plugs 10 into r for a 10-inch ball. Correction: before writing any formula, write “r = ___” on its own line and halve the diameter if needed.

Using slant height for volume. Correction: draw the right triangle inside the cone or pyramid; h is the straight-up leg, s is the slanted hypotenuse. Volume always uses h.

Forgetting the 1/3. Students compute a cone as πr2h. Correction: point out that a cone fits inside a cylinder and holds only a third of it. Have students circle the 1/3 on their formula sheet.

Mixing up p and B. In SA = ph + 2B, students put the base area where the perimeter belongs. Correction: p is a length (add the sides); B is an area (multiply). Label each with its units.

Scaling area or volume by k instead of k2 or k3. Correction: convert each length to real size first, then compute. Or show that doubling the edges of a cube gives 8 small cubes, not 2.

Wrong units or mixed units. Correction: volume answers are cubic, area answers are square. If one measurement is in inches and another in feet, convert before computing.

Differentiation

Support: Cut open an empty cereal box and lay it flat (a net) so students can see surface area as six rectangles. Give a formula sheet with the letters already color-coded (B in one color, p in another, h and s in a third). Let students use a calculator throughout and focus on choosing the formula and the numbers. Start with prisms only, then add one new solid at a time.

Stretch: (1) A cylinder holds 471 in3 and has a radius of 5 in. Find its height. (471 = 3.14 × 25 × h, so 471 = 78.5h and h = 6 in.) (2) A rocket model is a cylinder (radius 3 cm, height 10 cm) topped by a cone (radius 3 cm, height 4 cm). Find the total volume. (3.14 × 9 × 10 = 282.6; (1/3) × 3.14 × 9 × 4 = 37.68; total 320.28 cm3.) (3) An open-top box (no lid) is 8 in by 5 in by 3 in. How much cardboard does it take? (Full SA = 26 × 3 + 2 × 40 = 158; minus the missing top, 40, gives 118 in2.)

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Ask three of the checks above. Then have each student finish this sentence aloud or in the chat: “Before I use a formula, I always check ______.” (Good answers: radius or diameter; height or slant height; the units.) Preview the exit ticket and this week's study plan, including this week's Practice GED.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • The formula sheet is provided. Students can open it during the math test. Questions test whether they choose the right formula and the right measurements, not whether they memorized anything.
  • The on-screen calculator has a π key. Some questions say “use 3.14 for π,” some ask for an answer “in terms of π” (for example, 36π), and some give rounded answer choices. Teach students to read that instruction before computing.
  • Question formats. Multiple choice with four options (wrong choices often come from using the diameter, the slant height, or forgetting 1/3); fill-in-the-blank with rounding instructions (“to the nearest tenth”); drop-down menus that complete statements about formulas; drag-and-drop to sort or match.
  • Typical wording. “How many cubic feet of water can the tank hold?” “How much material is needed to cover…?” “On the blueprint, 1 inch represents 6 feet. What is the actual area?” “If each dimension is doubled, what happens to the volume?”
  • Working backward. Some items give the volume and ask for a missing height or radius. Students substitute what they know and solve the one-step equation.
student:
Welcome to Week 6

Last week you found perimeter and area of flat shapes. This week you go three-dimensional. You will find how much a box, can, cone, or ball holds (volume) and how much material covers it (surface area). Good news: on the GED you do not have to memorize these formulas. A formula sheet is provided. Your job is to read it correctly and put the right numbers in the right places.

1. Volume or Surface Area?

Volume is the space inside a solid. It answers “How much does it hold?” Units are cubic: in3, ft3, cm3.

Surface area is the total area of all the outside surfaces. It answers “How much material covers it?” Units are square: in2, ft2, cm2.

Water in a fish tank, soil in a planter, or air in a ball is volume. Paint on a shed, wrapping paper on a box, or a label on a can is surface area.

2. How to Read the Formula Sheet

The formula sheet uses a few letters over and over. Learn what they mean and the formulas become easy to use.

LetterWhat it means
BThe area of the base. Find it with the area formula for the base shape. A rectangle base: B = length × width. A circle base: B = πr2.
pThe perimeter of the base: the distance around the base. Add the sides.
hThe height: the straight-up distance from the base to the top, at a right angle to the base.
sThe slant height: the distance from the tip of a pyramid or cone down its slanted side to the edge of the base. It is always longer than the height.
rThe radius: half the diameter.
πPi, about 3.14. Use the π key on your calculator or 3.14, whichever the question tells you.
SolidVolumeSurface area
Rectangular prismV = BhSA = ph + 2B
CylinderV = πr2hSA = 2πrh + 2πr2
PyramidV = (1/3)BhSA = ½ps + B
ConeV = (1/3)πr2hSA = πrs + πr2
SphereV = (4/3)πr3SA = 4πr2

Three-line method: (1) Write the formula. (2) Rewrite it with your numbers in place of the letters. (3) Compute, and write the units. Before step 2, ask: “Do I have the radius or the diameter? The height or the slant height?”

3. Prisms and Cylinders

A rectangular prism (a box) and a cylinder (a can) both have two matching bases, one on the bottom and one on top. Their volume is the base area times the height: V = Bh. For a cylinder the base is a circle, so B = πr2 and V = πr2h.

Example 1. A storage bin is 3 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2.5 ft tall. Find its volume and surface area.

B = 3 × 2 = 6 ft2

V = Bh = 6 × 2.5 = 15 ft3

p = 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 ft

SA = ph + 2B = 10 × 2.5 + 2 × 6 = 25 + 12 = 37 ft2

Answer: V = 15 ft3; SA = 37 ft2

Example 2. A water tank is a cylinder with a radius of 2 m and a height of 5 m. Use 3.14 for π. How much water can it hold?

V = πr2h

V = 3.14 × 22 × 5 = 3.14 × 4 × 5

V = 62.8 m3

Answer: 62.8 cubic meters

4. Pyramids and Cones

A pyramid or cone rises from its base to a single point. It holds exactly one third of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height. That is why their volume formulas have (1/3) in front.

Height or slant height? Volume always uses the height h (straight up the middle). Only the surface-area formulas for pyramids and cones use the slant height s (down the outside). If a problem gives you both, use each one in the right place.

Example 3. A paper cup is shaped like a cone with a radius of 4 cm and a height of 9 cm. Use 3.14 for π. Find its volume.

V = (1/3)πr2h

V = (1/3) × 3.14 × 42 × 9 = (1/3) × 3.14 × 16 × 9

(1/3) × 9 = 3, so V = 3.14 × 16 × 3 = 3.14 × 48 = 150.72 cm3

Answer: 150.72 cubic centimeters

Example 4. A square pyramid has base edges of 10 ft, a height of 12 ft, and a slant height of 13 ft. Find its surface area and volume.

Base: B = 10 × 10 = 100 ft2; p = 4 × 10 = 40 ft

SA = ½ps + B = ½ × 40 × 13 + 100 = 260 + 100 = 360 ft2 (slant height)

V = (1/3)Bh = (1/3) × 100 × 12 = 400 ft3 (height)

Answer: SA = 360 ft2; V = 400 ft3

5. Spheres

A sphere is a ball shape. The only measurement you need is the radius. If you are given the diameter, divide by 2 first. Remember that r3 means r × r × r.

Example 5. A ball has a diameter of 12 inches. Use 3.14 for π. Find its volume.

r = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 in, and 63 = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216

V = (4/3)πr3 = (4/3) × 3.14 × 216

216 ÷ 3 = 72, and 72 × 4 = 288, so V = 3.14 × 288 = 904.32 in3

Answer: 904.32 cubic inches

6. Scale Drawings and Scale Factors

A scale drawing (a map, blueprint, or model) shows a real object smaller or larger, with every length changed by the same amount. A scale like 1 in : 8 ft means 1 inch on the drawing stands for 8 feet in real life.

  • To find a real length, multiply the drawing length by the scale (or set up a proportion).
  • To find a real area or volume, change each length to real size first, then use the formula.
  • If every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, area is multiplied by k2 and volume by k3. Double the sides of a box and it holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times as much.

Example 6. A model car is built at a scale of 1 : 24. The model is 7.5 inches long. How long is the real car, in feet?

Real length = 7.5 × 24 = 180 inches

180 ÷ 12 = 15 feet

Answer: 15 feet

Try It

Use 3.14 for π. Work on paper, then check.

1. Find the volume of a box that is 12 in long, 5 in wide, and 3 in tall.

Show answer

B = 12 × 5 = 60; V = 60 × 3 = 180 in3.

2. Find the volume of a cylinder with a radius of 5 cm and a height of 4 cm.

Show answer

V = 3.14 × 52 × 4 = 3.14 × 25 × 4 = 3.14 × 100 = 314 cm3.

3. A cone has a diameter of 10 ft and a height of 6 ft. Find its volume.

Show answer

r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. V = (1/3) × 3.14 × 25 × 6 = 3.14 × 25 × 2 = 3.14 × 50 = 157 ft3.

4. Find the surface area of a sphere with a radius of 3 m.

Show answer

SA = 4 × 3.14 × 32 = 4 × 3.14 × 9 = 12.56 × 9 = 113.04 m2.

5. On a blueprint with a scale of 1 in : 8 ft, a wall is 2.25 inches long. How long is the real wall?

Show answer

2.25 × 8 = 18 feet.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Volume is the space inside (cubic units). Surface area is the total outside area (square units).
  • On the formula sheet, B is the area of the base, p is the perimeter of the base, h is the height, s is the slant height, and r is the radius.
  • Prisms and cylinders: V = Bh. For a cylinder, B = πr2.
  • Pyramids and cones hold 1/3 of the matching prism or cylinder: V = (1/3)Bh.
  • Volume uses the height. Only pyramid and cone surface area uses the slant height.
  • Sphere: V = (4/3)πr3 and SA = 4πr2. Halve the diameter to get the radius.
  • In scale problems, change lengths to real size first. A scale factor of k multiplies area by k2 and volume by k3.

Exit Ticket

Use 3.14 for π.

1. Find the volume of a rectangular prism that is 7 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm.

Show answer

V = 7 × 4 × 2 = 56 cm3

2. Find the volume of a cylinder with a radius of 1 ft and a height of 10 ft.

Show answer

V = 3.14 × 12 × 10 = 31.4 ft3

3. In the pyramid formula SA = ½ps + B, what does s stand for?

Show answer

The slant height: the distance from the tip down the middle of a side face to the edge of the base.

4. Find the surface area of a sphere with a radius of 10 in.

Show answer

SA = 4 × 3.14 × 102 = 4 × 3.14 × 100 = 1,256 in2

5. A map scale is 1 cm : 50 m. Two buildings are 3.2 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they?

Show answer

3.2 × 50 = 160 m

Reflection

  • Which letter on the formula sheet (B, p, h, s, or r) was the hardest for you to keep straight? What will help you remember it?
  • Think of three objects in your home or workplace. For each one, would you ever need its volume, its surface area, or both? Why?
  • Look back at one problem you missed. Was the error choosing the wrong formula, using the wrong measurement, or a calculation mistake?

vocab.def: The amount of space inside a solid figure, measured in cubic units.
vocab.example: A box 2 ft by 3 ft by 4 ft has a volume of 24 ft<sup>3</sup>.

vocab.def: The total area of all the outside surfaces of a solid, measured in square units.
vocab.example: A cube with 2-inch edges has 6 faces of 4 in<sup>2</sup>, so SA = 24 in<sup>2</sup>.

vocab.def: A solid with six rectangular faces, like a box.
A solid with two matching circular bases connected by a curved side.
vocab.example: A soup can or a water tank.

vocab.def: A solid with a flat base (often a square) and triangular faces that meet at one point.
vocab.example: A square pyramid has 1 square base and 4 triangle faces.

vocab.def: A solid with a circular base and a curved side that narrows to one point.
vocab.example: An ice cream cone or a traffic cone.

vocab.def: A perfectly round solid in which every point on the surface is the same distance from the center.
On the formula sheet, B is the area of the base of a solid.
vocab.example: For a cylinder with r = 3, B = π × 3<sup>2</sup> = 9π.

vocab.def: The distance around the base of a solid; a length, not an area.
The straight-up distance from the base to the top or tip, at a right angle to the base.
vocab.example: A can that stands 10 cm tall has h = 10 cm.

vocab.def: The distance from the tip of a pyramid or cone down its slanted side to the edge of the base; used only in their surface-area formulas.
vocab.example: A cone with h = 4 and r = 3 has s = 5.

vocab.def: The distance from the center of a circle or sphere to its edge; half the diameter.
vocab.example: A ball with a 12-inch diameter has r = 6 in.

vocab.def: Units for volume, written with a small 3.
A drawing, map, or model in which every length is changed by the same amount from the real object.
vocab.example: On a floor plan with scale 1 in : 4 ft, 3 inches stands for 12 feet.

vocab.def: The number every length is multiplied by to go from one figure to a similar one.
vocab.example: A scale factor of 3 makes area 9 times and volume 27 times as large.

CylinderV = πr2hSA = 2πrh + 2πr2Radius, not diameter
PyramidV = (1/3)BhSA = ½ps + Bh for V, s for SA
ConeV = (1/3)πr2hSA = πrs + πr2h for V, s for SA
SphereV = (4/3)πr3SA = 4πr2r3 = r × r × r

Steps for Any Solid

  1. Name the solid. Volume or surface area?
  2. Find it on the formula sheet.
  3. Write r = ___, h = ___, s = ___, B = ___, p = ___.
  4. Substitute, compute, and write units.
  5. Round only at the end, as the question asks.

Scale

  • Scale 1 in : 4 ft → real length = drawing length × 4.
  • Change lengths to real size first, then find area or volume.
  • Scale factor k: lengths × k, area × k2, volume × k3.
  • Double the edges → 4 times the area, 8 times the volume.

Quick Examples (π = 3.14)

SolidMeasurementsResult
Box10 × 6 × 4 inV = 240 in3; SA = 248 in2
Cylinderr = 3 cm, h = 10 cmV = 282.6 cm3
Square pyramidedge 6 m, h = 4 m, s = 5 mV = 48 m3; SA = 96 m2
Coner = 3 in, h = 4 in, s = 5 inV = 37.68 in3; SA = 75.36 in2
Spherer = 5 cmSA = 314 cm2; V ≈ 523.3 cm3

Top mistakes: using the diameter as r; using s for volume; forgetting the 1/3 for pyramids and cones; putting an area where p (a perimeter) belongs; scaling area or volume by k instead of k2 or k3; square units for volume.

items.prompt: A fish tank is shaped like a rectangular prism. It is 30 inches long, 12 inches wide, and 16 inches tall. What is the volume of the tank?
items.hint: Use V = Bh. The base is the 30 by 12 rectangle.
items.explain:
Use V = Bh.

Area of the base: B = 30 × 12 = 360 in2

V = 360 × 16 = 5,760 cubic inches

2,064 is the surface area: 2(30 × 12) + 2(30 × 16) + 2(12 × 16) = 720 + 960 + 384 = 2,064. That measures the glass, not the space inside. 360 is only the base area (the height was left out). 58 comes from adding the three dimensions.

items.prompt:
The GED formula sheet gives the surface area of a pyramid as

SA = ½ps + B

What does the letter p stand for?
options: The slant height of the pyramid
items.hint: On the formula sheet, B is an area and p is a length. Which length goes all the way around the base?
items.explain:
On the formula sheet, p is the perimeter of the base: the distance around the base. For a square base with 6-inch sides, p = 4 × 6 = 24 inches.

The other letters in the formula: s is the slant height and B is the area of the base. The height h does not appear in this formula at all; it is used in the volume formula V = (1/3)Bh.

“The area of the base” is the most common wrong choice, but that is what B stands for.

items.prompt: Drag each task into the correct category. Does the task call for finding volume or surface area?
choices: Water needed to fill a swimming pool
Paint needed to cover the outside of a shed
Wrapping paper needed to cover a gift box
Soil needed to fill a planter
Leather needed to cover a basketball
Concrete poured into a cylinder-shaped post form
items.hint: Ask: is the material going inside the object (filling it) or on the outside (covering it)?
items.explain:
Volume measures what fills the inside of a solid. Surface area measures what covers the outside.

  • Water filling a pool: volume
  • Paint covering a shed: surface area
  • Wrapping paper covering a box: surface area
  • Soil filling a planter: volume
  • Leather covering a basketball: surface area
  • Concrete filling a post form: volume

A common slip is to put the basketball under volume because a ball is “full.” But the leather only covers the outside, so it is surface area.

items.prompt: On a road map, 1 inch represents 15 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the towns?
items.hint: Each inch stands for 15 miles. Multiply the map distance by 15.
items.explain:
Each inch on the map stands for 15 miles, so multiply:

3.5 × 15 = 52.5

Check with a proportion: 1/15 = 3.5/x, so x = 3.5 × 15 = 52.5 miles.

18.5 comes from adding 3.5 + 15. 45 comes from using only the 3 whole inches (3 × 15). 4.3 comes from dividing 15 by 3.5.

items.prompt:
A rain barrel is shaped like a cylinder. It has a diameter of 4 feet and a height of 6 feet. What is the volume of the rain barrel?

Use 3.14 for π. Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
items.hint: The formula needs the radius. What is half of the diameter?
items.explain:
Formula: V = πr2h

The radius is half the diameter: r = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 ft

V = 3.14 × 22 × 6 = 3.14 × 4 × 6 = 3.14 × 24 = 75.36

Rounded to the nearest tenth: 75.4 cubic feet

If you use the diameter, 4, as the radius, you get 3.14 × 16 × 6 = 301.44, which is four times too large.

items.prompt:
Choose the word or expression that correctly completes each statement about the formula sheet.

In the cone volume formula V = (1/3)πr2h, the letter h stands for the {{0}} of the cone.

In the pyramid surface-area formula SA = ½ps + B, the letter s stands for the {{1}}.

For a cylinder, the base is a circle, so the area of the base, B, is equal to {{2}}.
items.hint: Volume formulas use the straight-up height. B always means an area, and the area of a circle is on the formula sheet.
items.explain:
First blank: Volume formulas use the height, the straight-up distance from the base to the tip. The slant height is used only for surface area.

Second blank: In SA = ½ps + B, s is the slant height, the distance from the tip down the middle of a side face to the edge of the base. It is easy to think s means “side,” but the side length of the base is used to find p.

Third blank: B is the area of the base. A cylinder's base is a circle, and the area of a circle is πr2. That is why the cylinder volume formula V = πr2h is the same as V = Bh. The expressions 2πr and πd are the circumference (a length), and 2πrh is the area of the curved side.

items.prompt:
A planter is shaped like a cone. Its radius is 6 cm, its height is 8 cm, and its slant height is 10 cm, as shown.

About how much soil can the planter hold?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 60 190 A 90 22 0 0 0 240 190 A 90 22 0 0 0 60 190' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='20' x2='60' y2='190' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='20' x2='240' y2='190' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='20' x2='150' y2='190' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150' y1='190' x2='240' y2='190' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='150,180 160,180 160,190' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='156' y='115' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>8 cm</text><text x='178' y='184' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>6 cm</text><text x='205' y='100' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>10 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: A cone standing on its circular base. A dashed line from the tip straight down to the center of the base is labeled 8 cm and meets the base at a right angle. A dashed radius from the center to the edge of the base is labeled 6 cm. The slanted side from the tip to the edge of the base is labeled 10 cm.

items.hint: Volume uses the height (8 cm), not the slant height. Do not forget the 1/3.
items.explain:
Formula: V = (1/3)πr2h. Volume uses the height, 8 cm.

V = (1/3) × π × 62 × 8 = (1/3) × π × 36 × 8

(1/3) × 36 = 12, and 12 × 8 = 96, so V = 96π

96 × 3.14 = 301.44 (with the π key, 301.59). The answer is about 301 cubic centimeters.

About 377 comes from using the slant height, 10, instead of the height: (1/3) × π × 36 × 10 = 120π. About 904 comes from forgetting the 1/3 (288π). About 1,206 comes from using 12, the diameter, as the radius.

items.prompt:
A wooden block is shaped like a square pyramid. Each edge of the square base is 16 cm. The height of the pyramid is 6 cm, and the slant height is 10 cm, as shown.

What is the total surface area of the pyramid, including the base?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40,220 240,220 290,175 165,30' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='240' y2='220' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='40' y1='220' x2='90' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='90' y1='175' x2='290' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='90' y2='175' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='165' y2='197' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='165,187 175,187 175,197' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='165' y1='30' x2='140' y2='220' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='2,3'/><text x='171' y='150' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>6 cm</text><text x='143' y='150' text-anchor='end' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>10 cm</text><text x='120' y='244' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>16 cm</text></svg>
figure.alt: A square pyramid. The front edge of the square base is labeled 16 cm. A dashed line from the top straight down to the center of the base meets the base at a right angle and is labeled 6 cm. A dotted line from the top down the middle of the front face to the middle of the front base edge is labeled 10 cm.

items.hint: Use SA = ½ps + B. Find p (the distance around the base) and B (the area of the base). Surface area uses the slant height.
items.explain:
Formula: SA = ½ps + B

Perimeter of the base: p = 4 × 16 = 64 cm

Area of the base: B = 16 × 16 = 256 cm2

Slant height: s = 10 cm (surface area uses s, not h)

SA = ½ × 64 × 10 + 256 = 320 + 256 = 576 square centimeters

Check: each triangle face has area ½ × 16 × 10 = 80, and 4 × 80 = 320. Add the base: 320 + 256 = 576.

448 comes from using the height 6 instead of the slant height (½ × 64 × 6 + 256). 320 leaves out the base. 1,536 comes from using the base area 256 in place of the perimeter (½ × 256 × 10 + 256).

items.prompt: Select two solids that have a volume of exactly 36π cubic units.
options: A sphere with a radius of 3
A cylinder with a radius of 3 and a height of 4
A cone with a radius of 3 and a height of 4
A cylinder with a diameter of 6 and a height of 2
A sphere with a diameter of 3
A cone with a radius of 3 and a height of 6
items.hint: Leave π as π. Halve any diameter before you use the formula, and remember the 1/3 for cones.
items.explain:
Find each volume, leaving π in the answer:

  • Sphere, r = 3: (4/3)π × 33 = (4/3)π × 27 = 36π Correct
  • Cylinder, r = 3, h = 4: π × 32 × 4 = π × 9 × 4 = 36π Correct
  • Cone, r = 3, h = 4: (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π (one third of the matching cylinder)
  • Cylinder, diameter 6 so r = 3, h = 2: π × 9 × 2 = 18π
  • Sphere, diameter 3 so r = 1.5: (4/3)π × 1.53 = (4/3)π × 3.375 = 4.5π
  • Cone, r = 3, h = 6: (1/3)π × 9 × 6 = 18π

The two solids with volume 36π are the sphere with radius 3 and the cylinder with radius 3 and height 4. Choosing the cone with radius 3 and height 4 means the 1/3 was forgotten.

items.prompt: A landscaper's drawing of a rectangular patio uses the scale 1 inch : 6 feet. On the drawing, the patio is 2.5 inches wide and 4 inches long. What is the actual area of the patio?
items.hint: Change each length on the drawing to real feet first. Then multiply length by width.
items.explain:
Change each drawing length to real feet:

Width: 2.5 × 6 = 15 ft

Length: 4 × 6 = 24 ft

Area: 15 × 24 = 360 square feet

Check with the scale factor: the drawing area is 2.5 × 4 = 10 in2, and area grows by 62 = 36, so 10 × 36 = 360.

60 comes from multiplying the drawing area by 6 instead of 36. 78 is the perimeter (2 × 15 + 2 × 24), not the area. 10 is the area of the drawing, not of the real patio.

items.prompt: A small gift box is a rectangular prism 5 inches long, 4 inches wide, and 2 inches tall. A larger box is made by multiplying each dimension of the small box by a scale factor of 3. What is the volume of the larger box?
items.hint: Find the new length, width, and height first, or multiply the small volume by 3 × 3 × 3.
items.explain:
Small box: V = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 in3

Larger box dimensions: 5 × 3 = 15, 4 × 3 = 12, 2 × 3 = 6

V = 15 × 12 × 6 = 180 × 6 = 1,080 cubic inches

Check: volume grows by 33 = 27, and 40 × 27 = 1,080.

120 comes from multiplying the volume by 3 only. 360 comes from multiplying by 32 = 9, which is the rule for area. 280 comes from adding 3 inches to each dimension (8 × 7 × 5) instead of multiplying by 3.

items.prompt:
A grain silo is shaped like a cylinder with a hemisphere (half of a sphere) on top, as shown. The cylinder and the hemisphere both have a radius of 10 feet. The cylinder is 30 feet tall.

What is the total volume of the silo? Use 3.14 for π. Round your answer to the nearest cubic foot.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='100' y='80' width='100' height='150' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M 100 80 A 50 50 0 0 1 200 80' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='80' x2='200' y2='80' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='158' y='98' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>10 ft</text><line x1='80' y1='80' x2='80' y2='230' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='74' y1='80' x2='86' y2='80' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><line x1='74' y1='230' x2='86' y2='230' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='70' y='160' text-anchor='end' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>30 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A silo drawn as a rectangle (the side view of a cylinder) with a half circle on top. A dashed radius across the top of the cylinder is labeled 10 ft. A measurement line beside the cylinder, from its top to its bottom, is labeled 30 ft.

items.hint: Find the cylinder volume and the sphere volume separately. A hemisphere is half of a sphere. Then add.
items.explain:
Cylinder: V = πr2h = 3.14 × 102 × 30 = 3.14 × 100 × 30 = 9,420 ft3

Hemisphere: a full sphere is V = (4/3)πr3 = (4/3) × 3.14 × 1,000 = 12,560 ÷ 3 ≈ 4,186.67 ft3

Half of it: 4,186.67 ÷ 2 ≈ 2,093.33 ft3

Total: 9,420 + 2,093.33 = 11,513.33

Rounded to the nearest cubic foot: 11,513 cubic feet

If you add the whole sphere instead of half, you get 13,606.67, about 13,607. If you forget the hemisphere, you get only 9,420.

If you used the π key instead of 3.14, an answer of 11,518 or 11,519 is also accepted.
